nameStory: The scarlet oak earned its fiery name from its spectacular fall foliage, which blazes brilliant scarlet-red across New England's autumn landscape. This dramatic color display is so reliable and intense that early botanists chose 'scarlet' over other red-themed names to capture the tree's autumn glory.
description: Scarlet oak is a medium to large deciduous tree that can reach 60-80 feet tall with a broad, open crown. It's a member of the red oak group, known for its deeply lobed leaves that create beautiful patterns of light and shadow. The tree has a straight trunk with dark, furrowed bark and develops a distinctive branching pattern that makes it stand out in both forest and landscape settings.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply cut leaves with 7-9 pointed lobes separated by deep, rounded sinuses (indentations) that extend more than halfway to the midrib. The lobes end in sharp bristle tips you can feel with your finger, and the leaf feels thin and papery compared to white oak leaves.

idTips.label: Fall Color
idTips.description: Brilliant scarlet-red fall color that's more intense and uniform than most other oaks. The entire crown often turns the same vivid red, creating a stunning display that's visible from far away.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Dark gray to nearly black bark with deep furrows and flat-topped ridges. On younger trees, the bark is smoother and lighter gray, while mature trees develop thick, deeply fissured bark that feels rough and corky.

idTips.label: Acorns
idTips.description: Oval acorns about 1/2 to 3/4 inch long, sitting in deep cups that cover about half the nut. The acorn cap has tightly overlapping scales and often has a slight rim around the edge where it meets the nut.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Develops an open, irregular crown with spreading branches. Often has a clear central trunk when young but may develop multiple large branches as it matures, creating a broad, somewhat rounded canopy.

habitat: Scarlet oak thrives in well-drained, acidic, sandy soils and is commonly found on dry ridges, slopes, and upland areas throughout New England. It's often a key species in oak-heath forests, growing alongside other oaks, hickories, and understory plants like mountain laurel and blueberries. You'll frequently spot it on rocky hillsides and in mixed hardwood forests where the soil tends to be drier.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge with a reddish tinge in late April to early May, and small, inconspicuous flowers appear as hanging catkins (male) and tiny reddish clusters (female) around the same time.
seasonality.summer: Leaves are bright green and provide excellent shade, while small green acorns begin developing from pollinated flowers.
seasonality.fall: The spectacular scarlet-red fall color peaks in mid to late October, and mature acorns drop to the ground in their second year of growth.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the tree's distinctive growth pattern, and you can identify it by its dark, deeply furrowed bark and any persistent acorn caps on the ground beneath.

funFact: Scarlet oak is the official tree of Washington, D.C., chosen not just for its beauty but because it can tolerate urban pollution and compacted soils better than many other large trees, making it perfect for city life.
confusionNotes: Scarlet oak is most often confused with northern red oak, but scarlet oak's leaf lobes are separated by much deeper, more rounded indentations (sinuses), making the leaf look more 'cut up' or delicate. Remember: scarlet oak leaves look like they've been more deeply carved, while red oak leaves have shallower, more U-shaped indentations.
contextualKnowledge: Like all members of the red oak group, scarlet oak acorns take two years to mature and have a bitter taste due to high tannin content, unlike the sweeter acorns of white oak group species that mature in one year.
compareHints: Among New England's red oaks, scarlet oak stands out with its deeply dissected leaves that have the most pronounced sinuses (indentations). Northern red oak has similar bristle-tipped lobes but shallower cuts between them, while black oak leaves are often broader and less deeply lobed. The fall color is also a dead giveaway - scarlet oak's brilliant red is more intense and uniform than the variable browns and reds of its oak relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England oaks, white oak is distinguished by its evenly rounded leaf lobes without bristle tips (unlike red oak group species) and its light gray bark.

Among New England's oaks, northern red oak is distinguished by its pointed leaf lobes (white oak has rounded lobes), its large size (much bigger than bear oak or dwarf chinkapin oak), and its relatively shallow acorn caps (deeper than scarlet oak, shallower than pin oak).
Bear oak stands apart from other New England oaks by being consistently shrubby rather than tree-like, even at maturity.
Among the red oak group, black oak has the deepest leaf lobes - much deeper than red oak or pin oak.
Unlike white oak with its deeply rounded lobes, chestnut oak has scalloped edges with rounded teeth.
Among New England's white oak group, swamp white oak is unique in its preference for wet areas and its distinctive leaf shape with deeper bottom lobes.
Unlike other New England oaks that have lobed leaves (deeply indented edges), dwarf chinkapin oak has simple leaves with rounded teeth like a saw blade.
English oak stands out among New England's oaks by having the leaf and acorn stems completely reversed from most natives - very short leaf stems but very long acorn stems.
Among New England oaks, pin oak stands out for its combination of deeply-cut leaves with sharp points and its distinctive pin-like branching pattern.
Among New England oaks, bur oak is easily distinguished by its enormous acorns with fringed caps and extremely deeply-lobed leaves.
Among New England oaks, post oak is unique for its cross-shaped leaves with rounded lobes and fuzzy undersides.
Unlike most New England oaks, chinkapin oak has toothed rather than lobed leaves, setting it apart immediately from white oak, red oak, and others.
Unlike our native oaks, Turkey oak has those telltale bristly buds and bristle-tipped leaves that you can actually feel.
Sawtooth oak is completely different from all other New England oaks because of its simple, toothed leaves rather than the lobed leaves found on species like white oak, red oak, or black oak.
Among New England oaks, willow oak is unmistakable due to its unlobed, willow-like leaves - all other regional oaks have distinctly lobed or toothed leaves.
Among New England oaks, shingle oak is instantly recognizable by its simple, unlobed leaves - all other common oaks in the region have the typical lobed leaves we associate with oaks.
